make sure to stay close to exit
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
issues.explanation: This item is not well aligned with the rest of the profile or the cognitive formulation. The active formulation is dominated by a Triggers–Threat–Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Negative Appraisals inactive. In contrast, punishment/self-deserving-suffering is a negative self-appraisal theme rather than a threat-management strategy, and it does not connect plausibly to the selected trigger and threat items. The other maladaptive strategies (avoiding emotional stress, staying near exits) fit the trigger-threat-hypervigilance pattern, but punishment thinking pulls toward a different clinical profile that is otherwise not represented.

vignette:
Carlos, a sixty-five-year-old special education teacher, had been a medic in the Army during the Gulf War. The event that now governed his life had not been a firefight, but a heat-stroke evacuation gone wrong inside a sweltering aid station. He had been helping to stabilize a soldier with a fever of 105 when the man suddenly seized and stopped breathing. As Carlos worked the bag-valve mask, he tasted something metallic and sweet—the soldier’s blood from a bitten tongue, mixed with the chemical tang of the ammonia inhalants he was snapping under the man’s nose. Then the dizziness hit him, a spinning, tilting vertigo that made the canvas walls of the tent buckle. He remembered thinking, I’m going down too, and the terror was not for the soldier but for himself—the shame of being a medic who could not hold steady. The soldier died. Carlos was evacuated for heat exhaustion, but the taste and the dizziness never really left him.

In the decades since, Carlos had built a careful life around those two sensations. He worked as a special education teacher in a public middle school, a job that required patience, structure, and proximity to children who sometimes made sudden, loud sounds. He had learned to manage by staying near the classroom door. Every morning, before the first student arrived, he would walk the perimeter of the room, checking that the door was unobstructed, that he could step into the hallway in three seconds. He kept his desk at the back corner, farthest from the windows, so that no one could approach him from behind. He had come to believe that if he could not see an exit, the dizziness would return and he would fall, and that this time he would not get back up.

The taste appeared without warning. Sometimes it happened when a student unwrapped a piece of gum, or when the cafeteria served something with a metallic aftertaste. He would excuse himself, walk quickly to the staff bathroom, and rinse his mouth with water until the flavor faded. His colleagues had noticed. The principal had asked, gently, if he was feeling unwell. He had laughed it off—allergies, he said—but he knew they were watching him differently.

His hypervigilance had become a constant companion. In the hallway between classes, he scanned the faces of students, the angles of open locker doors, the shadows behind water fountains. He identified escape routes in every room he entered: the library, the auditorium, the faculty lounge. He could not sit in a restaurant booth; he needed a table near the door, his back to the wall. When a fire alarm drill sounded, he felt his heart hammer and his vision narrow, and he had to grip the doorframe to keep from bolting. He had learned to avoid situations that made him feel strong emotions—anger, excitement, even joy—because he was certain that any emotional spike would bring back the dizziness and the taste, and he would lose control.

He had been divorced for fifteen years. His ex-wife had said he was never present, that he was always looking over her shoulder, always restless. She had been right. He had not dated since. He lived alone in a small apartment with a clear line of sight to the front door. He did not own a television because the sudden sounds of action movies or news reports triggered the alertness that left him exhausted by noon.

What finally brought Carlos to seek help was a morning in late October. A student with autism, overwhelmed by a math worksheet, had begun to scream—a high, sustained shriek that filled the classroom. Carlos had frozen, his mouth filling with that old metallic sweetness, his vision swimming. He had stumbled toward the door, left the room, and stood in the hallway shaking. Another teacher had to take over. He drove home that afternoon and called the clinic. He was most afraid that this was not something therapy could fix, that the taste and the dizziness were now part of who he was. But he was also hoping—quietly, without letting himself believe it—that he might one day sit through a full meal with a friend, or walk through a crowded hallway without checking every door.
